raw_case_text:
The patient was a 39-year-old Mozambican citizen who had been residing in Johannesburg. He reported multiple visits to Mozambique bi-annually, usually 3-4 weeks at a time. He had no known comorbidities and was previously well. He reported multiple previous episodes of malarial infection, the last of which was 2 years prior, treated with oral medication.
He had been in Mozambique for the last 3 weeks, where he developed fever and vomiting, which lasted 10 days, followed by non-bloody diarrhoea. He presented at a local clinic in Mozambique, where he was diagnosed with malaria and received outpatient treatment. He received four tablets twice a day for 3 days - which is in keeping with our presumption of artemether and lumefantrine ('Coartem'). He returned to Johannesburg during his last day of treatment. On previous occasions, he would improve within days; however, after the completion of the treatment, he experienced worsening dyspnoea, fever, jaundice and macroscopic haematuria for 5 days. Thereafter, he presented to Helen Joseph Hospital Casualty.
On examination, the patient was pale, the blood pressure was 168/98 mmHg, the pulse rate was 121 beats per minute, the temperature was 37.8  C and the respiratory rate was 36 breaths per minute using accessory muscles, indicating significant respiratory distress. This is in association with an oxygen saturation of 85% on ambient air, which did not improve on face mask oxygen at a fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) of 60%. On systemic examination, the liver was enlarged (2 cm), with a smooth surface, and was non-pulsatile. On inspection of the urine sample, there was macroscopic haematuria confirmed as blood on the urine dipstick.
Laboratory investigations showed haemolysis evidenced by a haemoglobin decrease from 10 g/dL on admission to 4 g/dL (after 3 days), with a macrocytosis of 104 fL, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) of 2425 U/L (normal range 15-40), an unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (total bilirubin 35 micromol/L and conjugated bilirubin 17 micromol/L) and a lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) of > 3500 U/L (normal range 100-190) (see Table 1).
During the first 3 days of admission, the patient developed temperature spikes between 38.4  C and 38.8  C. The patient was in respiratory distress with a respiratory rate of 24-36 breaths per minute. There were no obvious respiratory signs on clinical examination or abnormalities on the chest X-ray, as seen in Figure 1. The patient was admitted to the high care unit and was initiated on intermittent haemodialysis.
The first arterial blood gas determination demonstrated a discrepancy between the reading of the pulse oximeter (85%) and the blood gas co-oximeter, which showed an oxygen saturation of 99.6%. The difference in the saturations can be explained by the methaemoglobin level of 12.4% demonstrating that this patient has methaemoglobinaemia, as seen in Table 2.
On day 2 of hospitalisation, an urgent blood smear was done, showing significant blister cells and Heinz bodies. In association with the haemolysis, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency was suspected (see Figure 2 and Figure 3). The smear was negative for malaria and confirmed on a pan-malarial polymerase chain reaction.
A septic screen was done as part of the initial workup, including blood, urine and stool cultures. On day 6 of admission, the stool culture was positive for Salmonella typhi, as seen in Figure 4 (colonies are colourless and transparent with black centres as seen by black arrow), Figure 5 (colonies are red with black centres as seen by blue arrow) and Figure 6 (colonies are grey as seen by green arrow).
Supportive management, including intermittent haemodialysis, supplementary oxygen, fluids, blood products and targeted antibiotic (ceftriaxone), was the mainstay of treatment. Specific treatments for methaemoglobinaemia, such as methylene blue and high-dose ascorbic acid, were both relatively contraindicated because of the ongoing haemolysis and renal dysfunction in this clinical case. The patient subsequently improved and was discharged with full recovery. The patient was counselled on precautionary measures for G6PD deficiency, such as avoiding fava beans, mothballs and the use of aspirin. He was also counselled to let healthcare workers know if seeking medical advice that he has a G6PD deficiency.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 39-year-old male presented with a 5-day history of worsening dyspnea, persistent fever, jaundice, and macroscopic hematuria following a febrile diarrheal illness in Mozambique.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: While in Mozambique for 3 weeks, the patient developed fever and vomiting lasting 10 days, followed by non-bloody diarrhea. He attended a local clinic where he was empirically treated for malaria with oral artemether/lumefantrine (four tablets twice daily for 3 days), returning to Johannesburg on the final treatment day. Following completion of antimalarial therapy, he developed progressive dyspnea, persistent fever spiking between 38.4 °C and 38.8 °C, jaundice, and gross hematuria over 5 days, prompting emergency presentation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Mozambican citizen residing in Johannesburg, with bi-annual visits to Mozambique for 3-4 weeks. No prior chronic medical illnesses. Reported multiple previous episodes of malaria, most recently 2 years prior, treated with oral medications.
subjective.review_of_systems: Worsening dyspnea, fever, jaundice, gross hematuria, nausea, vomiting, and non-bloody diarrhea.

objective.physical_examination: Pale, in significant respiratory distress with accessory muscle use. Blood pressure 168/98 mmHg, pulse rate 121 bpm, temperature 37.8 °C (spiking to 38.4-38.8 °C during early admission), respiratory rate 36 bpm (ranging 24-36 bpm), oxygen saturation 85% on ambient air refractory to 60% FiO2 via face mask. Abdomen: liver enlarged 2 cm below costal margin, smooth surface, non-pulsatile. Inspection of urine showed macroscopic hematuria. Respiratory examination revealed no focal chest signs.
objective.routine_investigations: Urine dipstick confirmed macroscopic hematuria. Hemoglobin decreased precipitously from 10 g/dL on admission to 4 g/dL over 3 days, with macrocytosis (MCV 104 fL). AST 2425 U/L (reference range 15-40), unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with total bilirubin 35 micromol/L and conjugated bilirubin 17 micromol/L, LDH >3500 U/L (100-190). Arterial blood gas revealed pulse oximetry saturation of 85% discordant with co-oximeter arterial oxygen saturation of 99.6%, with methemoglobin fraction of 12.4% (methemoglobinemia). Urgent peripheral blood smear on day 2 showed prominent blister cells and Heinz bodies, suggestive of G6PD deficiency. Peripheral blood smear and pan-malarial PCR were negative for Plasmodium species. Chest X-ray showed no focal pulmonary abnormalities.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Salmonella typhi infection (typhoid fever) confirmed by positive stool culture on day 6 of admission (demonstrating characteristic colourless colonies with black centres, red colonies with black centres, and grey colonies); complicated by acute intravascular hemolysis, severe hemolytic anemia, methemoglobinemia (12.4%), and acute renal failure secondary to underlying glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency triggered by typhoid infection and/or artemether-lumefantrine exposure. Acute malaria was ruled out by negative blood smear and pan-malarial PCR. Methylene blue and high-dose ascorbic acid were contraindicated due to G6PD deficiency and ongoing hemolysis/renal failure.
Plan & Outcome: Admitted to the high care unit and managed with intermittent hemodialysis, supplemental oxygen, IV fluids, packed red blood cell transfusions, and targeted antibiotic therapy with intravenous ceftriaxone. The patient demonstrated progressive clinical improvement, recovery of renal and hematological function, and was discharged in full recovery. Counselled regarding lifelong G6PD deficiency precautions (avoidance of fava beans, mothballs, aspirin, and oxidative medications).
